--- title: "Project 4: Capitec and the Big Four" subtitle: "A Kalman filter for a time-varying beta" toc: false number-sections: false execute: echo: false warning: false message: false --- ::: {.pf-meta} | | | |:----|:--------------------------------------------| | Section and topic | Part 2: State-space models and the Kalman filter | | Type of project | Implementation from first principles, with a model comparison, on real data | | Data used | Weekly total returns of Capitec (`CPI.JO`), Standard Bank, FirstRand, Absa and Nedbank (equal-weighted composite), and the JSE All Share, from Yahoo Finance. Period: Jan 2015 to Oct 2026 (616 weeks). All public aggregate market data, so no personal data and no POPIA consent issue. | | Methods used | Time-varying regression as a state-space model (random-walk beta, with and without drift); Kalman filter, smoother and likelihood coded by hand and validated against OLS and the `dlm` package; boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test; profile likelihood; one-step forecast comparison with a Diebold-Mariano test against constant and rolling regressions; robustness to price returns, the market regressor, dropping Absa and sub-samples. | ::: ## Question Has Capitec's share price become less tied to the Big Four banks over time, as a disruptor story would predict? ## Key findings

best forecast MSE ratio vs OLS
- **Time variation.** The boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test of a constant beta gives $p$ = 0.222, and the weekly standard deviation of the beta's change is 0.0079. - **Drift.** The beta drifts by 0.002 per year (95% interval -0.067 to 0.070), from 0.80 to 0.82 over the sample. The interval includes zero, so the data do not establish a drift. - **Robustness.** 0 of 3 whole-sample alternatives (price returns, the All Share as regressor, the composite without Absa) also show a drift below zero. - **Forecasting.** The lowest one-step forecast error comes from Expanding OLS, with an MSE ratio of 1.000 against expanding-window OLS. - **Estimator check.** The hand-coded filter matches OLS to within 1.7e-09 when the state noise is switched off. **What this does and does not show.** A falling beta means Capitec has become less tied to the Big Four. It is not proof of disruption, because earnings growth, valuation or ownership changes would produce the same pattern. ![Left: Capitec's smoothed beta to the Big Four (blue, with 95% band) against a 104-week rolling regression (grey) and the constant OLS beta (dashed). Right: profile likelihood for the standard deviation of the beta's weekly change.](figures/p4_headline.png){fig-alt="Two panels: the time-varying beta with a band and a rolling estimate, and the profile likelihood for the beta volatility."} ## What I would do differently I would use a Student-t or GARCH observation error, because the Gaussian errors ignore the volatility clustering I found in Project 1. I would add the market as a second time-varying regressor so the Big Four beta is net of the market, and use market-cap weights in the composite. ## Detailed analysis [Read the detailed analysis →](analysis.html){.pf-button} Code and data: [Code & Data appendix](../../appendix/code-and-data.qmd).
